name: Simancas
summary: A fortress town on the Duero near Valladolid where Ramiro II of León destroyed the caliphal army of Abd al-Rahman III in 939, and which later housed the central archive of the Spanish crown.
overview: Simancas guarded a crossing of the Duero on the tenth-century frontier between León and the Caliphate of Córdoba, and its name belongs to the greatest Christian victory of that century.
knownFor: The Battle of Simancas in July 939
The frontier of the Duero between León and Córdoba
The castle that became the General Archive of Simancas
The last campaign Abd al-Rahman III led in person

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Simancas — the Roman Septimanca — stands above the Duero a little downstream of Valladolid, at a crossing that mattered because the river was the frontier. In the tenth century the line of the Duero divided the Kingdom of León from the Caliphate of Córdoba, and Simancas was one of the strongpoints holding it.

The town is remembered for a single summer. In July 939 the campaigning army of Abd al-Rahman III came north to break the Leonese frontier and was destroyed near the town, in a defeat so complete that the caliph never again took the field in person.

contentSections.title: The campaign of 939
paragraphs: Abd al-Rahman III had proclaimed himself caliph in 929 and spent the following decade making Córdoba the dominant power in the peninsula. The expedition of 939 was conceived on a grand scale, a campaign of overwhelming force intended to settle the northern frontier, and the caliph led it himself.

Against him Ramiro II of León assembled an unusually broad coalition: his own forces, the Castilian count Fernán González, and García Sánchez I of Pamplona. The armies met near Simancas around 19 July 939. Both sides recorded a solar eclipse as the fighting began, which unnerved them equally — and which gives the battle one of the few independently checkable dates in tenth-century Iberian warfare.

contentSections.title: The rout and the ditch
paragraphs: The caliphal army broke after several days of fighting and was pursued south-east across the plain. The pursuit ended at a ravine the Arabic sources call al-Khandaq, the ditch of Alhándega, where a large part of the retreating force was trapped and killed.

Abd al-Rahman escaped narrowly, and the extent of the disaster is measured by what he left behind: his personal copy of the Qur'an and his gilded coat of mail were taken on the field. He had several hundred of his own commanders crucified afterwards for their conduct, among them Fortún ibn Muhammad, the governor of Huesca, who had held his troops back from the battle.

contentSections.title: What it settled, and did not
paragraphs: The victory secured the Duero line for a generation and allowed León and Castile to consolidate settlement south of the river. Ramiro II's reputation rested on it for the rest of his reign.

It did not break Córdoba. The caliphate recovered, and under the chamberlain al-Mansur in the later tenth century it raided Christian Spain more destructively than ever, sacking León, Barcelona and Santiago de Compostela. What Simancas changed permanently was the caliph's own practice: after 939 Abd al-Rahman III directed campaigns through his generals and never commanded in the field again.

contentSections.title: The castle and the archive
paragraphs: The medieval castle was rebuilt in the fifteenth century by the Enríquez admirals of Castile and passed to the crown. In 1540 Charles V ordered the royal papers to be gathered there, and Philip II's instruction of 1561 turned it into a permanent, purpose-organised institution — the first state archive of its kind in Europe.

The General Archive of Simancas still holds the central records of the Castilian and Spanish monarchy from the fifteenth to the eighteenth centuries. For a place whose fame rests on one battle, it is a peculiar afterlife: the fortress that guarded a frontier became the building in which the empire that grew out of that frontier kept its memory.

timeline.title: Abd al-Rahman III takes the caliphal title
timeline.description: Córdoba asserts itself as a caliphate and presses the northern frontier through the 930s.

timeline.title: Battle of Simancas
timeline.description: Ramiro II, with Fernán González and García Sánchez I, destroys the caliphal army near the town.

timeline.title: The ditch of Alhándega
timeline.description: The pursuit traps much of the retreating army in a ravine; the caliph loses his Qur'an and mail.

timeline.title: The crucifixions
timeline.description: Abd al-Rahman executes commanders he blames for the defeat and never again leads an army in person.

timeline.title: The castle rebuilt
timeline.description: The Enríquez family reconstructs the fortress, which later passes to the crown.

timeline.title: The royal archive
timeline.description: Charles V orders the crown papers gathered here and Philip II makes the archive permanent.

imageInfo.caption: The castle of Simancas above the town on the Duero, rebuilt in the fifteenth century and later the seat of the crown archive, in a 2017 photograph.
imageInfo.creator: Heparina1985 (Wikimedia Commons)
imageInfo.note: The fabric shown is later than the battle. The tenth-century stronghold that Ramiro II defended was rebuilt as a fifteenth-century castle by the Enríquez family and remodelled again in the sixteenth century to hold the royal records, so the towers here belong to the archive rather than to the frontier fortress of 939.
